findings.title: Posted workers: two new expense items missing from the national list
findings.euChange: The amendment added host-state accommodation conditions and reimbursement for professional journeys within the posting assignment to Article 3(1). It requires equal treatment where host-state entitlements exist, not universal employer-provided accommodation.
findings.consequence: Possibly. Slovenia’s core list for workers posted into the country does not name the two added items. Other national expense rights and the broader rules for longer postings may supply protection. Their equivalence has not been fully assessed, and no missing entitlement or refused reimbursement has been established.
findings.nationalGap: The Commission identified inbound coverage concerns in 2024. Current ZDR-1 Article 210(2) still omits the two heads; Article 3(3) applies ZDR-1 to inbound foreign-law contracts through its posting provisions. Article 130 supplies ordinary employee expense rights and Article 139 preserves accommodation already agreed as remuneration, but neither has been established as a universal initial inbound route. Separate foreign-worker housing standards also exist.
findings.caveat: This is a coverage lead, not an established denial of rights. The 2015 foreign-worker housing regulation provides living and hygiene standards in covered employer-provided accommodation. Longer postings receive broader rights after 12 months, or 18 after a motivated extension, under Article 210(6)–(7). Collective agreements, overriding mandatory rules and the complete housing framework were not exhaustively audited.
findings.provisions: EU 2018/957 Article 1(2)(a), adding Directive 96/71 Article 3(1)(h), (i); SWD(2024)320 section 3.1.1.4.4; national ZDR-1 Article 210(2).
findings.resolution: We found no official correction since 2024 adding these two items to the list for workers posted into Slovenia. The 2026 consolidated text still leaves them out, but whether Slovenian law as a whole falls short has not been verified.

findings.title: Jam: national decree lagged behind the EU’s higher fruit minimums
findings.statusLabel: Government-admitted delay · October 2026 concern
findings.statusDetail: The government admitted the delay
findings.summary: Belgium has admitted that its jam decree is late. In October 2026 the Commission reported that Belgium had not fully notified its measures.
findings.euChange: Article 3(4) and Annex II(1)(a) raised the general fruit-content minimum per 1,000 g of finished ordinary jam from 350 g to 450 g, and extra jam from 450 g to 500 g. Specific fruits have separate thresholds. Article 5 required national adoption/publication by 14 December 2025 and application from 14 June 2026.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. Belgium’s 2004 rules set the old minimums (350 g of fruit per kg of ordinary jam, 450 g for extra jam). Belgium has admitted that its replacement is late and it was still forthcoming in July 2026; we have not treated the draft as enacted. Jam placed on the market or labelled before 14 June 2026 may still be sold until stocks run out, and the Commission’s opinion is an allegation of incomplete notification, not a judgment.
findings.nationalGap: The 2004 decree used general minima of 350 g/kg for ordinary jam and 450 g/kg for extra jam. The Economy Ministry said its replacement remained forthcoming on 3 June 2026; a written ministerial answer on 8 July confirmed a delay involving national fruit-spread rules and the EU technical-notification process. The current official Justel body, read on 26 October 2026, still displays the earlier general minima; no repeal or amendment was shown in its header.
findings.nationalLaw: Royal Decree 19 March 2004 on manufacture and marketing of jams, jellies, fruit marmalades, chestnut purée and fruit spreads, Article 1§2; replacement decree pending in the government’s July 2026 account.
findings.provisions: Directive 2024/1438 Article 3(4), Annex II(1)(a), Articles 5–6; Belgian 2004 decree Article 1§2(1)(a),(2)(a).
findings.resolution: An official EU notification draft (TRIS) contains the new minimums. On 1 October 2026 the Commission sent a reasoned opinion saying no measures had been notified for the jam rules. We found no enacted replacement; lack of notification alone does not prove that no law exists.
findings.caveat: The government’s June/July statements establish a historical legislative delay. The October 2026 Commission reasoned opinion is an allegation about incomplete notification, not a judgment or conclusive evidence of continued legislative absence. No claim is made that every jam sold is non-compliant: Article 6 allows products placed on the market or labelled before 14 June 2026 to be sold until stocks are exhausted. Special-fruit thresholds also differ. The draft is not treated as enacted law.

comparison.after: 450 g per kg of ordinary jam; 500 g per kg of extra jam.
comparison.note: General minima only; special fruits have other thresholds, and pre 14 June 2026 stock has an express transition.
comparison.afterLabel: New EU minimums (also in the Belgian draft)

findings.title: Hazardous waste: an economic exception the EU removed is still in national law
findings.statusLabel: Current national exception · correction remains a draft
findings.statusDetail: Ministry draft would delete the exception
findings.evidenceLabel: National text checked
findings.summary: Germany still lets companies skip separating illegally mixed hazardous waste if separation is economically unreasonable. The ministry proposes deleting this exception.
findings.euChange: Article 1(16) replaced Article 18(3). Unlawfully mixed hazardous waste must be separated where technically feasible and necessary for Article 13 environmental and health protection. The earlier EU text expressly mentioned economic feasibility; the replacement omits that qualification.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. German law still lets operators skip separating unlawfully mixed hazardous waste when that is economically unreasonable, which the revised EU rule no longer mentions. This concerns only unlawfully mixed hazardous waste, not ordinary household waste, and the ministry itself proposes deleting the exception. Whether any operator used it, or any harm resulted, was not checked.
findings.nationalGap: Current KrWG Section 9a(3), sentence 2, permits transfer to an authorized treatment facility when separation is economically unreasonable. The ministry proposes deleting that exception as incompatible with the revised EU rule.
findings.nationalLaw: Kreislaufwirtschaftsgesetz Section 9a(3), sentence 2; proposed amendment Article 1(9).
findings.provisions: Directive 2018/851 Article 1(16), replacing Directive 2008/98 Article 18(3); Article 2(1) deadline.
findings.resolution: The proposed deletion is still in a ministry draft. The ministry’s process page, updated 30 September 2026, aims for Cabinet consideration in January 2027. The official national text, checked on 25 October 2026, still contains the exception.
findings.caveat: This concerns unlawfully mixed hazardous waste, not all separate collection or ordinary household waste. No individual operator’s use of the exception or resulting harm was checked. The ministry’s incompatibility assessment is not a court judgment. A proposed deletion is not an enacted fix.

findings.summary: Irish Regulation 6(4) still treats solid biomass used in plants below 20 MW as meeting the sustainability criteria. The EU threshold has fallen to 7.5 MW, and the official amendment register shows no change to the Irish rule.
findings.euChange: Solid-biomass criteria start at 7.5 MW.
findings.nationalGap: S.I.350/2022 Regulation 6(4) deems solid biomass fuels used in installations with total rated thermal input below 20 MW to fulfil the sustainability and greenhouse-gas criteria. Regulation 6(10) limits financial-support eligibility to compliant fuels; Regulation 8 establishes SEAI's verification procedure by reference to Regulation 6. The official amendment register records many later changes to S.I.350/2022 but none to Regulation 6 or Schedule 3. This leaves the express automatic-compliance provision covering the 7.5–less-than-20 MW band newly covered by the EU amendment.
findings.nationalLaw: European Union (Renewable Energy) Regulations (2) 2022, S.I.350/2022, Regulations 6(4), 6(10) and 8; official chronological amendment table updated to 13 October 2026.
findings.provisions: RED III Articles 1(19)(a)(iii), 5(1); RED Article 29(1),(15); national Regulation 6(4).
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. Ireland’s automatic exemption covers plants between 7.5 and 20 MW that the EU now includes. Whether any subsidy decision, fuel delivery or miscounted plant has been affected has not been established.
findings.resolution: We found no Irish law changing Regulation 6(4) and no official acknowledgment of this mismatch. The SEAI verification page still points operators to S.I. 350/2022 and the RED II criteria. A separate SEAI report had already described the EU threshold falling to 7.5 MW in 2025; that shows awareness of the EU change, not an admission that Irish law omitted it.
findings.caveat: This is a statutory-text lead. The criteria govern renewable-energy accounting, obligations and support, rather than general permission to burn biomass. Article 29(15) preserves old criteria until 31 December 2030 for qualifying support granted before 20 November 2023, with fixed long-term amounts and an anti-overcompensation mechanism; focus on installations outside that route. Separate scheme conditions, EU ETS requirements and verification practice need further review. The official amendment register stops 13 October 2026; targeted later-enactment searches found no correction.

comparison.before: Solid biomass used below 20 MW counts as meeting the sustainability and greenhouse-gas criteria automatically.
comparison.after: The criteria apply from 7.5 MW (with exceptions).
comparison.note: Focus on the 7.5–less-than-20 MW band outside qualifying pre-November-2023 support.

findings.review: Two agents independently checked the authentic EU amendment, original Irish regulation, official amendment table updated to 13 October 2026, the listed 2025–26 amendments and current SEAI verification instructions. Both checked Article 29(15) grandfathering and searched for standalone overriding legislation. No contrary threshold amendment located; actual scheme conditions and individual installations remain unverified.
findings.recognitionNote: No official acknowledgment of the exact surviving Irish Regulation 6(4) mismatch located. SEAI has publicly described the new EU threshold; Ireland's general RED III transposition issues are already public. No claim of first discovery or of an unrecognized directive-wide delay.

findings.statusLabel: Current omission · corrective draft published
findings.statusDetail: Government draft published for consultation
findings.summary: A 2026 EU amendment allows three specific uses of cobalt in toys. Hungary’s list of permitted substances still names only nickel. A government draft published in October proposes adding cobalt, after the EU’s implementation dates.
findings.euChange: Article 1 adds three cobalt uses to Annex II Appendix A: stainless steel as a nickel impurity, electrical-conducting components, and neodymium magnets that cannot be swallowed or inhaled. Article 2 requires publication by 29 July 2026 and application from 29 August.
findings.nationalGap: Annex 2 Appendix A of Decree 38/2011 lists only nickel. Part III point 4.3 requires Commission approval and Appendix A listing for that permission route. The separate low-concentration and inaccessibility alternatives in points 4.1–4.2 remain available.
findings.nationalLaw: 38/2011. (X. 5.) NGM rendelet a gyermekjátékok biztonságáról, Annex 2 Part III points 3–4 and Appendix A; current official NJT version dated 31 December 2022.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. Hungary’s list does not yet include the new EU permission for cobalt uses that cannot rely on the low-concentration or inaccessibility exceptions. No rejected product or enforcement consequence has been established.
findings.caveat: The amendment permits specified uses; it does not generally relax all cobalt restrictions. Existing concentration and inaccessibility exceptions still apply. Directive-consistent interpretation and EU free-movement rights may protect compliant products despite the national text. No claim of unsafe toys, actual trade obstruction or deliberate disregard is made. The new Toy Safety Regulation does not fully replace these rules until 2030.

findings.resolution: The current official text, checked on 25 October, still lists nickel only. findings.review: Independent verifier directly read current NJT, checked the absent row and all alternative exceptions, the authentic EU application date and targeted later-enactment searches. The chain passed with a caveat against claiming that all cobalt toys are banned.

findings.nationalLaw: Real Decreto 56/2016, Articles 2(1)–(2) and 3(1); live BOE consolidation, latest amendment published 2 June 2021.

findings.title: Lead exposure: national limits still at the earlier, higher values
findings.statusLabel: Current statutory limits · legislation pending
findings.statusDetail: Legislation pending
findings.summary: Italy’s current lead limits are still the earlier ones, after the April 2026 deadline. Parliament’s records show the government acknowledging that implementation is late.
findings.euChange: The revised limits are 0.03 mg/m³ over eight hours and, through 2028, 30 µg Pb/100 ml in blood. Earlier-exposure exceptions apply.
findings.nationalGap: Annex XLIII retains 0.15 mg/m³ for inorganic lead and its compounds. Annex XLIII-bis retains a blood-lead limit of 60 µg Pb/100 ml. Both values appear in the inspectorate-hosted October 2026 compilation and match the authentic 2024 enactment.
findings.nationalLaw: Legislative Decree 81/2008, Annexes XLIII and XLIII-bis, as amended by Legislative Decree 135/2024, Article 21 and Annexes B–C.
findings.provisions: EU Article 3(1) and Annex II(2)–(3); national Annex XLIII lead row and Annex XLIII-bis point 1.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. Italy’s numerical limits for lead are higher than the new EU limits. Employers’ general duties on prevention, substitution and keeping exposure low still apply, and this does not mean that any particular workplace exposure is lawful, or that anyone was harmed.
findings.resolution: The national register (Normattiva), read on 25 October, lists its latest amendment as published on 23 March 2026. A Senate document (Dossier 768) records the government’s explanation of the delay and a pending delegation of power to legislate. We found no later implementing act.
findings.caveat: The inspectorate-hosted October compilation disclaims official status; authentic Gazette tables and the current amendment register corroborate it. Workers already above 30 but below 70 due to pre-9-April-2026 exposure may continue under regular surveillance if levels decline towards 30. The 2029 limit is not today’s requirement. No court ruling on this comparison is claimed.

comparison.before: Air: 0.15 mg/m³ over eight hours. Blood: 60 µg lead per 100 ml.
comparison.after: Air: 0.03 mg/m³. Blood: 30 µg per 100 ml (transitional).

findings.review: Two agents independently verified the exact EU and authentic Gazette values, the October compilation and current Normattiva register. findings.summary: Italy lowered its threshold for solid biomass to 7.5 MW, but for now lets plants in the newly covered band count and receive support without checking the sustainability criteria, until implementing decrees are adopted and in any case no later than 30 June 2027.
findings.euChange: Article 30(6) allows simplified checks ensuring compliance.
findings.nationalGap: Legislative Decree 199/2021 Article 42(16), replaced by Decree 5/2026 Article 20(n), permits electricity and heat from solid biomass in 7.5–20 MW plants to count towards national objectives/obligations and access support without verification of Article 42(5)–(12), pending simplified-certification decrees and no later 30 June 2027. findings.nationalLaw: Legislative Decree 199/2021 Article 42(16), as replaced by Legislative Decree 5/2026 Article 20(n); current official Finance Ministry reproduction, in force 4 February 2026.
findings.provisions: RED III Articles 1(19), 1(21)(e), 5(1); national Article 42(16),(18-ter).
findings.consequence: Yes, until the decrees are adopted (30 June 2027 at the latest). Italy lets plants of 7.5–20 MW count and receive support without verification, which looks broader than the simplified verification the EU requires. National Article 42(3), support-scheme conditions, EU ETS requirements and voluntary certification may independently impose protections. Permitting simplified audits is different from proving any particular automatic-compliance policy unlawful. Current decree status requires monitoring because an implementing decree could end this transition before its stated outer date.

comparison.after: Compliance must be ensured through simplified verification.

findings.summary: Cyprus’s asbestos regulations still use the earlier limit, ten times the new EU limit. Replacement rules had still not been published when we checked on 25 October 2026, after the implementation deadline.
findings.euChange: Article 1(7) replaces Article 8: the eight-hour limit becomes 0.01 fibres/cm³. Article 2(1) makes this due by 21 December 2025; the separate 2029 derogation does not cover that initial limit.
findings.nationalGap: Regulation 4 of KDP 316/2006 specifies 0.1 fibres/cm³ over eight hours. The 2015 amendment leaves that provision untouched. The ministry’s October 2026 legislation page continues to list these instruments.

findings.provisions: EU Article 1(7), inserted Article 8(1), and Article 2(1)–(2); national Regulation 4.
findings.consequence: Yes, on paper. The national limit is ten times the new EU limit. Employers’ wider duties to prevent and minimise exposure still apply; comparing the numbers does not show that exposure at any particular site is lawful, or that anyone was injured.
findings.resolution: On 22 September 2026 the minister acknowledged the delay and said replacement regulations had been sent to Parliament. A parliamentary committee discussed them on 20 October. No asbestos instrument appears in the latest Gazette (23 October), and searches found no published replacement.
findings.caveat: This concerns the limit already due, not the separate measurement changes due in 2029. The 2015 instrument gives more-favourable carcinogen provisions priority; no alternative national provision imposing the revised asbestos limit was located. No claim of an actual unsafe workplace or individual injury is made.

findings.title: Extra-jelly table uses ordinary-jam quantities after the EU increase
findings.summary: Czechia raised extra-jam fruit minima to 500 g per kilogram generally, but its new extra-jelly row uses the lower ordinary-jam quantities: 450 g generally. The EU still links extra jelly to extra jam.
findings.nationalGap: Current Decree 397/2021 Section 5(6) points directly to Annex 1. Its extra-jelly row specifies 450/350/180/230/80 g for general fruit, the specified fruit group, ginger, cashew apples and passion fruit. The EU-linked extra-jam quantities are 500/450/280/290/100 g. Current official inspectorate guidance repeats the lower general and special-group figures.
findings.nationalLaw: Decree 397/2021, Sections 2(1)(i), 5(6) and 7(1), Annex 1; replaced by Decree 358/2025 Article I point 26, applicable from 14 June 2026.
findings.consequence: A newly produced extra jelly could satisfy the written Czech quantity table while falling below the EU minimum. For ordinary fruit, the difference is 50 g per kilogram; special-fruit differences vary. No such product was identified.
findings.review: An independent researcher personally read the authentic EU amendment, original jelly links and the enacted Czech amendment table. The parent separately read the current official consolidation, operative table hook, all relevant amendment points and full version history. Czech-language authentic EU texts were also checked.
findings.recognitionNote: Bounded Czech and English searches on 27 October 2026 found laws, guidance and reform descriptions, but no precise published criticism of this discrepancy. The parent and a peer each read the whole disclosed Commission comments in TRIS 2025/0218/CZ: these concern mutual recognition of non-harmonised foods, not jelly quantities. The parent also read the whole Czech reply and separate Commission message reserving transposition assessment for its conformity check. Any unpublished assessment remains unknown; this does not establish first discovery.

comparison.before: 450 g generally for extra jelly; 350 g for the specified fruit group.
comparison.after: 500 g generally for extra jelly; 450 g for the specified fruit group, through the unchanged extra-jam link.
comparison.note: Amounts per kilogram of finished product; extract-preparation water is deducted. Special ginger, cashew and passion-fruit thresholds also differ.

findings.title: Jam quantities increased, but both jelly rows retain the old minima
findings.summary: Slovakia updated the jam and extra-jam rows but left its jelly and extra-jelly fruit quantities unchanged. Its current binding table still gives general minima of 350 g and 450 g per kilogram, against EU-linked minima of 450 g and 500 g.
findings.nationalGap: Decree 44/2012 Section 3(1) directs manufacturers to Annex 1. Rows 1–2 now use the increased jam quantities; rows 3–4 retain all five previous jelly quantities. The 399/2025 amendment changes weights only in rows 1–2, although it edits some names in all four rows.
findings.nationalLaw: Decree 44/2012, Sections 2(j), 3(1) and Annex 1 rows 1–4; Decree 399/2025 Article I points 26–27 and Article II.
findings.consequence: After deducting preparation water, a new jelly made to the written Slovak minimum could contain 100 g less fruit juice or aqueous extract per kilogram than the EU-linked general minimum; for extra jelly the general difference is 50 g. No actual product or inspection outcome was established.
findings.review: The parent and an independent verification researcher each read the current binding table and the entire 399/2025 amendment. The parent also visually checked both table pages. A second researcher independently read the authentic EU amendment and original jelly cross-references; Slovak-language authentic EU texts were checked.
findings.recognitionNote: Bounded Slovak and English searches on 27 October 2026 combined jelly, the 2025 decree, the 2012 principal and the EU amendment, locating no precise published recognition of the residual jelly-table mismatch. The parent also read all 15 visible comment texts across both pages of official consultation LP/2025/584. They concern transition/packaging, names, drafting and concordance-table documentation; none identifies the retained jelly weights. Individual detail replies and every legislative attachment were not audited. This does not establish first discovery.

comparison.before: Jelly 350 g and extra jelly 450 g generally per kilogram; special-fruit rows also retain old values.
comparison.after: Jelly 450 g and extra jelly 500 g generally per kilogram, through their jam and extra-jam links.
comparison.note: The binding current PDF confirms the unchanged jelly rows. Extract-preparation water is deducted. The concern excludes protected earlier stock.

findings.title: The new jam rules keep pomegranates where the EU amendment specifies cashew apples
findings.summary: Slovenia raised its jam quantities in 2026 but retained “granatna jabolka” (pomegranates) in the special fruit category. The replacing EU text expressly uses “akažujeva jabolka” (cashew apples).
findings.nationalGap: The new national Annex 1 points 1–2 retain the old Slovenian EU term for pomegranates, although the authentic 2024 replacement uses cashew apples. Articles 2 and 4 make the national annex operative. The EU-reference clause in Article 1 does not itself rewrite that table.
findings.nationalLaw: Pravilnik o kakovosti in označevanju sadnih džemov, želejev, marmelad in sladkane kostanjeve kaše, SOP 2026-01-0809, Articles 1–7 and Annex 1 points 1–2.
findings.consequence: On the written national categories, pomegranate jam could use the special 230 g minimum rather than the EU general 450 g; extra jam could use 290 g rather than 500 g. Cashew apples could instead face the national general minima. These are potential recipe consequences; no actual product or enforcement outcome was established.
findings.review: The parent and a verification researcher independently read the whole six-page national rule, including all three annexes, and the authentic Slovenian original and replacing EU texts. The verifier separately checked the current official registry. Official Slovenian phytosanitary guidance independently identifies granatno jabolko as Punica granatum (pomegranate).
findings.recognitionNote: Bounded Slovenian and English searches on 27 October 2026 combined the two fruit names, the national rule identifier and the EU amendment. They found the legislation and general reform material, but no precise prior criticism of this retained fruit-name mismatch. This does not establish first discovery.

findings.statusLabel: Qualified omission · corrective draft under consultation
findings.statusDetail: A proposed cobalt entry is under consultation until 31 October 2026; its proposed 25 November commencement is not enacted law.
findings.evidenceLabel: Authentic EU amendment and actual national amendment chain read
findings.summary: Croatia’s toy-safety list still contains only nickel. The Ministry’s September draft would add the three specified cobalt uses, after the EU application date. Existing low-concentration and inaccessibility alternatives remain available.
findings.euChange: Adds three defined cobalt permissions; national application is required from 29 August 2026.
findings.nationalGap: Article 10(1) binds the national Annex II. Its Part III points 4(c) and 5(c) require both European permission and inclusion in national Appendix A. The 2015 replacement lists nickel only; the five later enacted amendments read do not add cobalt. A September 2026 ministry draft expressly proposes adding that entry to the currently applicable text.
findings.nationalLaw: Pravilnik o sigurnosti igračaka, NN 83/2014 Article 10 and Annex II Part III points 3–7/Appendix A; Appendix A replaced by NN 38/2015 Article 3. Later amendments: NN 35/2017, 50/2018, 60/2019, 48/2021 and 140/2022.
findings.consequence: For a specified cobalt use that cannot independently satisfy the low-concentration or inaccessibility exceptions, the written national list does not yet express the new permission. No actual product refusal, prohibited sale or trade obstruction was established.
findings.caveat: This is a qualified comparison of formal rules, not an adjudicated breach. Low-concentration and inaccessible-material alternatives, CE conformity presumptions, EU free-movement rights and directive-consistent interpretation may protect products. The draft is not a correction already in force. No unsafe-toy, actual refusal or deliberate-disregard claim is made. The new Toy Safety Regulation’s substantive replacement applies from 1 August 2030 and does not itself complete this current permission update.
findings.provisions: EU 2026/192 Articles 1–2;2009/48 Articles 12,15 and Annex II Part III points 3–7; national Article 10, Annex II Part III points 4(c)/5(c), Appendix A.
findings.resolution: The current ministry regulatory lists end with NN 140/2022. The 30 September 2026 draft adds cobalt and proposes force on 25 November 2026; consultation remains open until 31 October. Bounded official-register searches found no later enacted amendment by 27 October. The national text was reconstructed from actual originals and the complete officially listed amendment chain, not represented as a newly read official consolidation.
findings.recognitionNote: The Ministry’s draft and explanatory memorandum identify adding cobalt as the key difference from the currently applicable rule. This precise issue is already publicly recognized; no novelty claim is made.
findings.review: Verifier read the whole six-amendment national chain, current official ministry list, whole proposed amendment and explanatory memorandum, and authentic EU permissions. Reference independently read the principal scope and exception provisions, whole 2015 list replacement, whole latest 2022 amender, whole draft and authentic EU amendment. The final qualified source and prose reviews passed; no actual market restriction was established.
